# Coach's report — run 1, in-game 2005-03-16

Next game vs NYI on Friday 18 March 2005.

## Development opportunity

The question: are the young players getting the games they've earned? With 10 games left, this is the last window to answer it with action.

**Spezza** is the loudest case and his morale has now dropped to 86, the lowest on the young list. 37 games, 7.5 MPG, 15 points at POTE 99. I raised this five times before and the reading hasn't moved. At 21 with a 7.5 MPG season, the development case is dead unless he dresses for some of these last ten games. He should be active for the NYI game and any other game where we're comfortable. Reason class: development, but the morale at 86 makes it both.

**Colaiacovo** produced 12 points in 31 games, 0.39 per game, at 17.9 MPG when in the lineup. **Eminger** produced 21 in 54, also 0.39 per game, at 15.9 MPG. The rotation argument for keeping Eminger ahead no longer holds on production -- they're identical. Colaiacovo is 22 with POTE 99 and should get more of these last 10 games over Eminger on merit. Reason class: development.

**Stahle** played 4 games at 17.8 MPG per game. That's progress from zero games in January, and 17.8 MPG shows the coaches trusted him when they needed a body. But 6% share across the season at POTE 96 and age 20 is still thin. He's getting looks, not enough.

**Chlup** is earning everything: 50 points in 61 games at 16.5 MPG on the second line at 19. No concern. **Nash** at 35 points in 59 games on 12.7 MPG on the third line is a 20-year-old doing exactly what his role asks. **Gaborik** needs no development note at 85 points and 20.3 MPG.

**Klesla** plays all 72 games at 14.9 MPG, so minutes aren't the issue. His 0.38 pts/g at 22 is the concern, not usage. **Spacek** at 7.8 MPG on the fourth line at 19 is where he sits now. The 10 MPG target I set is unreachable and I've said so.

**Alexeev** is scratched despite 30 points in 55 games at 8.3 MPG. That's 0.55 per game on limited ice, one of the best rates on this list. If the lineup needs a body in the bottom six he's the obvious pick. **Ouellet** at 11 games as a third goalie is fine. **Koltsov** is the GM's chip, 18 points in 35, sitting at 49% share.

I'm delivering on task #1 (D sell-list update) in the matchup/roster phase this run, not here.

## Development trends

The window from December 1 to March 16 is long enough to separate trend from noise, and with 10 games left it is the last chance to change a young player's year before the offseason begins.

**Chlup** is the one still climbing. 0.62→0.88 pts/g on minutes from 11 to 18 at 19. Both went up, which at that age means the system is working. He belongs in the top nine permanently and I will keep giving him that ice. No change needed, confirmation only.

**Kaberle** went from 0.54 to 0.62 pts/g at 27 with minutes from 19.4 to 21.7. Most 27-year-olds get less and produce less. He is going the other way. First-pair confirmed for next year.

**Nash** is the young-player problem. 0.83→0.43 pts/g at 20 with minutes flat at 12.7. His rate halved with no change in role. That is not a minutes issue. Either he hit a wall or he is not suited to the job we gave him. I have no explanation from what I can see, but 35 games at 0.43 is enough of a sample to flag.

**Abid** went from 20.1 to 12.6 MPG while still producing 0.84 pts/g. A player scoring 0.84 per game does not belong on 12 minutes. That is a morale risk at 24, and his overall is still good enough to help. He needs more ice in the last 10 games.

**Upshall** is sitting at 5.3 MPG at 21 with a flat 0.32 rate. That is 46 points in 58 games spread over a benched role. Another wasted year unless we get him back to 10+ MPG in the final stretch, which is a low bar.

**Fischer** continues his quiet decline: 0.63→0.44 at 24 while his minutes went from 20.8 to 22.6. He is playing harder and producing less. The GM's keeper, so no trade call, but if next season opens the same way he is a planning problem on a four-year contract.

**Jackman** is confirmed: 0.65→0.38 at 24 on 30.4 MPG. His role cannot stay this way. The load is the problem.

**The aging veterans:** Sundin at 34 went 1.46→0.92 on 21.6 MPG. Mogilny at 36 went 1.62→0.84 on 19.2. Roberts at 38 went 1.29→0.81 on 21.3. All three are still playing top minutes with 30-50% less production than the season's start. The team is still leaning on them while Chlup and Nash play less. The plan for next season needs to decide who these three hand the ice to.

**Eminger** is trending up over the season (0.35→0.42 at 21 on 16.6 MPG) but his recent window is volatile. At 21 with an expiring deal he is still tradeable on the right night. No change until season's end.

## Morale watch

The room is healthy and no player's morale is being damaged by their ice time.

**Spezza** sits at 86, the lowest on the roster. He's scratched and his 7.5 MPG is a season average from limited early-game action. At 21 with 15 points in 37 games, he's below the 90 threshold where morale stops costing a grade point, but his change column reads "=" or "+1" consistently. The development scratch is the GM's call and his morale isn't collapsing, so I'm not overriding it.

**Spacek** is at 89, up 5 since the last save. His 7.8 MPG is below the 10 MPG band he'd expect at his calibre, but the trend is sharply positive and the season is winding down. The +5 suggests the March minutes bump registered. Let it ride; he's not a problem.

**Everyone else is at 92 or above.** Mogilny at 96 and trending up despite 18.4 MPG at 36, Richards at 96 on 16.6 MPG, Chlup at 96 on 16.5 MPG. No high-calibre player is simultaneously under his band and losing morale. The winning has done its work across the board.

No change for morale reasons tonight against New York.

## Role composition

**Are these units built for their jobs?** Yes, all of them. The checking, scoring and speed are distributed correctly across the four lines and both special teams units.

**L1** is the top line by every metric that matters: Sundin at 89 faceoffs anchors the dot, Roberts brings 82 checking and 89 clutch as the net-front presence, and Gaborik behind him is 97 scoring with 99 playmaking. The D pair of Jackman (88 checking) and Fischer (82 checking) means this line is the defensive anchor too. No gap.

**L2** has checking mean 68 and that's fine. Mogilny (92 scoring) and Afinogenov (90 scoring, 90 playmaking) are pure offensive wingers. Chlup at 78 faceoffs handles the dot. The auto-pair with McCabe at 82 checking on the back end covers the thin front end. This line exists to score.

**L3** is the matchup line. Richards at 95 clutch and 73 faceoffs is the best available draw man behind Sundin, and his checking on the displayed ratings is what gives L3 its 92 best. Chistov's 96 speed makes him a transition threat. Nash provides the physical body. This is the line that shuts people down.

**L4** checking mean 71 is fine for a depth unit. Abid at 70 toughness gives a body. The faceoff void (mean 50, best 51) is the known structural problem and the roster cannot fix it from here. No change.

**PK units** are the strongest part of the structure. K2 carries checking mean 82 with Jackman (88) and McCabe (82) both on it. K1 has Roberts and Fischer at 82 checking. Every PK unit has two players above 82 in checking. That's well-built.

**PP units** both have shooters. P1 leads with Gaborik and Sundin; P2 has Mogilny at 92 scoring and Richards for puck movement. Kaberle's 85 stamina makes him the engine on P1. Nothing to fix.

No composition change is warranted. The units are doing what they're built to do.

## Opponent matchup

The question: does NYI create a specific problem our current setup can't handle? No. We are 51-12-4 at home against a 26-33-4 team shooting 7.5% on the power play (17/227). The talent gap is too wide for a single line adjustment to matter.

**DiPietro** at 83 OVR is their best player tonight. Rebound control of 62 stands out. Our first line shoots high-event hockey already; against a goalie who gives up second chances, we should see more than 3-4 goals if we get volume. No adjustment needed for that, just shoot.

**Peca** at 85 OVR is the one player who creates a real problem. CHKG 88, AGGR 92, HERO 92, FACE 77. He is the best two-way center on their roster by a margin. Against our L2/D2 shift group (Chlup + Kaberle/McCabe), Kaberle's CHKG 68 and TOUG 55 make him a target. However, the auto-pairing only lets me change D slot order, and swapping Fischer/Jackman to D2 removes Jackman's SHPW 90 from the point when Sundin's top unit is on the ice. The offensive cost of that swap outweighs the defensive gain. McCabe CHKG 84 and Chlup CHKG 74 are enough to limit damage.

**Their PP is 17/227.** They will not score against our PK1 (Sundin/Roberts/Fischer/Kaberle) regardless of who we dress. No penalty-kill adjustment warranted.

**Their third pair** (Robidas 70, Martinek 71) against our L3 (Richards 85, Nash 81, Chistov 80) is our most favorable even-strength matchup. No change needed to exploit it; the existing pairing already gives us that.

**Decision: No change.** The record gap (116 vs 70 points, 3.40/1.40 vs 2.20/2.50), the PP gap (37.2% vs 7.5%), and the depth gap make this a game where playing our standard lines at full strength is the highest-probability path to two points. Development priority could apply here since we can afford it, but the GM has not taken the Spacek bump recommendation three times in a row, and repeating a recommendation he keeps declining is not productive.

**Obligation #1 — defenceman evaluation.** Updated sell order: Salo (0.18 pts/g, cheapest cut), Eminger (0.17 recent, expiring $1.2M), Klesla (0.38 season, declining at 22), Fischer ($3.7M x4 for 0.50 pts/g). McCabe stays off the list at 0.83. Jackman is not on the sell list but needs a reduced role next season; 0.48 pts/g on 30.4 MPG at age 24 means the load is the problem, not the player.

## Owed

**Defenceman evaluation and sell-list update for NYI game (game #11 of this duty):**

**Eminger** has continued to fall since I put him back on the sell list. Season rate is now 0.39 pts/g on 54 games (21 points). When I flagged him on Feb 26 he was at 0.44 season rate with a 0.17 recent window. That recent window has become his season. Expiring $1.2M at 21 with no recovery means he leaves as a cheap UFA this summer unless the GM moves him in the offseason before he walks. Most urgent sell on the blue line.

**Jackman** at 0.47 pts/g on 70 games, 30.3 MPG. Unchanged from the March 14 reading (0.48 on 69). The season is confirmed: he cannot hold that load and produce at his age and skill. Three years at $0.7M means no contract urgency, but his role must shrink next year or he becomes a liability on the back end at 25. This is a "change the role" problem, not a "sell now" problem.

**Klesla** unchanged at 0.38 pts/g on 72 games, 14.9 MPG. 22 years old, two years at $0.9M. Still a second-year decline. His trade value is his age and his money, not his production. The GM should shop him in the offseason before his third year forces a roster decision.

**McCabe** stays off the sell list. 58 points in 72 games = 0.81 pts/g. He was never coming back at 29, and he proved that by recovering. Four years at $3M is the cost of keeping him.

**Fischer** and **Kaberle** are untouchable per the GM's standing instructions.

What has changed since March 14: Eminger's season rate dropped from 0.44 to 0.39. Everything else is static. The sell order is Eminger, Klesla, and Jackman is a role-change case rather than a sell.

title: GM Assistant's report — run 1, in-game 2005-03-14

# GM Assistant's report — run 1, in-game 2005-03-14

Toronto 50-12-4, 114 pts after 71 games.

## Role coverage

Role coverage is solid across most categories, with two genuine thin spots: faceoffs (one player at 80+) and durability (four at 80+). The toughness line reads zero at 80+ on displayed grades, but this is the same form artifact confirmed on Feb 21: stored grades show six Toronto players above 80 TOUG, and the displayed number has never recovered. No trade needed for toughness.

**Sundin** at 90 FACE is the only faceoff winner on the roster. Richards moved to third-line centre on Feb 23 at 70 FACE, which is the best available internal option and was correctly placed. No other centre or wing exceeds 75. In a playoff series against a team with two 80+ centres, this gets exploited. This is the one genuine structural gap that needs external help.

**Jackman** at 87 CHKG displayed is the top checker, and the coach wants to cut his minutes because production is collapsing. The problem: no one else carries a checking grade close to his. Tucker at 83 CHKG is the next best and he is not lined. Cutting Jackman's load without dressing Tucker moves the minutes to Klesla or Colaiacovo, who check less. If the coach wants to reduce Jackman's minutes, Tucker must be activated on the same night.

**Durability** at four players above 80 (Roberts 98, Afinogenov 95, Fischer 92, Abid 90) is thin for a 71-game season heading into playoffs. The core scorers (Mogilny at 36, Sundin at 34, Roberts at 38) all sit below 80 in this category, which is expected at their ages, but it means a three-week injury stretch for any of the top six has no internal replacement. This is not fixable at the deadline; it is a summer drafting priority.

**Tucker** at 83 CHKG, 70 displayed TOUG, 29, not lined, is the free internal fix for the fourth checking role. He has been off the lineup all season. Dressing him solves the coach's Jackman-load problem and gives the bottom six a penalty-killer without any trade cost. This is the single most obvious internal roster-gap fix available.

**Goalies** are covered going forward. Luongo at 25 with 2 years left, 94 in both glove grades, is the starter. Belfour at 39, $6.50M, 1 year expiring is the trade asset per the Feb 21 GM order. Ouellet at 23 with 2 years is the backup. Tellqvist at 25, 1 year, $0.80M is the only expendable piece and saves nothing meaningful.

## Trajectory

The trajectory question is whether the July 2005 contract wall breaks the club or the club breaks through it. The answer is it breaks through, provided the GM sequences the renewals correctly and converts Belfour and Svehla into picks before the season ends.

**The age curve is healthy.** Fourteen players at 23 or under, twelve at 24-29, zero at 30-33, four at 34+. That gap between 29 and 34 means the club ages out all at once in a decade, not in three years. The immediate cliff is contractual, not biological.

**Belfour** is $6.50M, 92 base, 39 years old, 31 GP. His value peaks now because his 2.27 GAA and .916 save percentage make him the best playoff goalie available as a rental. The GM's Feb 21 instruction is to explore a return that is "good but locked on reasonable salary." That return should be a defenceman or forward under 28 with two or more years on a sub-$3M deal. He fills the 30-33 gap and recovers draft capital simultaneously.

**Sundin** is the immovable object: 34, $8.40M, five years left, POTE 60. He will be 39 when this contract expires. At 79 points in 71 games he is still good tonight, but the contract outlives the production by two or three years and weighs $8.40M on the payroll every season until 2010. Nothing to do about it now, but it means the young core must be locked cheap enough to carry his money alongside theirs.

**Fischer** is the one that hurts on a three-year view. $3.70M, four years, age 24, POTE 90 but producing 0.50 ppg in 66 games, down from 0.63 last season. The grades say he should be a top-four defenceman. The ice says he is a third-pair regular. This is $3.70M of dead money through 2009 that the GM cannot touch until 2008 at earliest. Flag it for a summer 2008 dump.

**The 13-player cluster at $21.30M** is the wall. Split it into three tiers at season end:

Tier 1 (lock 5-6 years): Gaborik 85 pts/$1.10M, Eminger POTE 99/$1.20M, Nash POTE 95/$1.20M, Richards 63 pts/POTE 88/$1.00M, Kaberle 38 pts/$1.90M. That's $6.50M now; expect $15-18M on long deals. Pay it; these are the franchise.

Tier 2 (lock 2-3 years): Chistov POTE 95/$1.10M, Alexeev POTE 94/$1.10M, Abid POTE 94/$0.40M, Upshall POTE 99/$1.20M, Colaiacovo POTE 99/$1.10M, Tellqvist POTE 91/$0.80M. These need development time before committing five years. Two-year deals at a modest raise cost maybe $7-9M total and re-enter the market in 2007 when we know who they are.

Tier 3 (walk): Belfour $6.50M (trade at deadline), Roberts $2.70M (38, POTE 52, expired function), Svehla $3.60M if still here (36, trade at deadline). That's $12.80M of salary leaving, which funds the Tier 1 raises.

**Draft capital is nearly empty.** One fourth-rounder, nothing better. This means every trade package must be funded by players, and Toronto has no future first to sell if a rebuild ever forces one. Belfour and Svehla are the only assets that can recover a first or second via the over-80 expiring mechanic. Failing to move both means entering 2005-06 with a single fourth-rounder and a roster that cannot be reshaped through the draft.

**The money has room.** $60.04M payroll against $88.37M revenue gives $24.72M of profit headroom. After removing the Tier 3 salaries and adding Tier 1 raises, net payroll increase is roughly $8-10M, putting Toronto at $70-75M. Still profitable at current revenue. The constraint is not money. It is whether the GM gets the Tier 1 players signed before someone else's AI offers them more in July.

## Calendar

The deadline is five days away and the decision is whether to pull the trigger on Belfour for Hejduk or let a $6.50M expiring asset walk in July for nothing. The answer is execute it now. Everything else at the deadline is secondary.

**Belfour → Colorado for Hejduk.** The GM already tested this on February 21 and Colorado said yes. Hejduk is 91 base, $2.50M, 2 years left, age 31. He passes every test the GM set on Feb 21: good (91 base), locked on reasonable salary ($2.50M), a couple of years into the future (2). Belfour at 39 and $6.50M walks in July if not moved by March 19. This trade converts a rental that will retire into a top-6 winger on a controlled deal. It is the single highest-value action available before the deadline and it requires no draft pick from Toronto.

**Roberts for a pick.** 38 years old, $2.70M, 87 base, expiring. He is over 80 and the GM has not protected him. The over-80 expiring mechanic means he can be traded for a draft pick to a non-playoff destination (per the March 4 order). If no deal is built by Friday, he simply walks in July and Toronto lose $2.70M of salary relief with no return. The action is to find a non-contender who needs a veteran winger and take whatever they offer. Even a fifth-rounder is better than nothing.

**Svehla is not expiring.** He does not appear on the current expiring list of 13. The February 23 note that flagged him as a pick-recovery candidate appears to be wrong about his contract status. He is not available for the over-80 mechanic. Drop that target.

**Havlat remains optional.** Tucker plus the 4th-rounder for Havlat (OTT, 23, 87 base, $900K expiring) is still available in theory. But with Hejduk already headed in via Belfour, the depth-scoring problem has its answer. Spending Tucker (who the GM values as physical depth) and the only pick Toronto owns (a 4th) on another 87-base winger is redundant. Skip it unless the GM specifically wants a second top-six addition.

**Summer renewals.** Thirteen contracts expire. Five are foundation players who need 5-6 year deals immediately at season's end: **Gaborik** (91 base, age 23, $1.10M), **Nash** (age 20, $1.20M), **Eminger** (POTE 99, age 21, $1.20M), **Kaberle** (27, $1.90M), **Richards** (24, $1.00M). These five are the team. If they cluster in July without extension talks, the core walks simultaneously. **Tellqvist** stays per the January 15 order (high-90s potential, give him time), renew on 3 years at a modest raise. **Abid** on 2-3 years at current salary. **Upshall, Chistov, Colaiacovo** on 3-4 years. **Alexeev** on 2 years as a prove-it deal at 23 with one year to show.

The GM owes himself a yes or no on Belfour in the next 48 hours. Colorado said yes to Hejduk. The window closes Friday.

## League scan

The deadline question for a team at 114 points with 11 games left is not "can we win without help" — it is "can we fix the one thing that gets exposed in a playoff series while our assets still have value." That thing is faceoff depth and third-line scoring. Belfour and Svehla are both expiring; if we don't move them now, we get nothing. Every target below fills a gap the role-coverage phase identified or converts an asset we'd otherwise lose in July.

**Havlat** (OTT, RW, 23, 87 base, 80 points in 63 games, $900K expiring) is the lead scoring target. OTT at 65 points with 11 expiring contracts and $32.13M profit are sellers. Package: Tucker plus the 4th-rounder. Tucker at 83 CHKG, 29, not lined, is free currency that gives OTT the physical presence they need. Losing Tucker costs us the internal Jackman-load fix, but the coach already has Colaiacovo moving up and Stahle dressing on the third pair, so the internal reshuffle absorbs it.

**Morris** (COL, D, 26, 85 base, 57 points in 65 games, $1.70M expiring) is the Belfour return that meets the GM's Feb 21 criterion: young, good, locked on reasonable salary. COL at 91 points are contenders, but Morris is expiring and they need a goalie. The March 5 note flagged this as better than Hejduk on every axis. The test: does COL value a playoff-ready goalie enough to give up their second-best scorer? If they won't give Morris, Hejduk is the fallback but fails the "locked for a couple years" test.

**Reid** (STL, RW, 23, 77 base, FACE 80, POTE 94, $600K expiring) closes the faceoff gap at the cheapest available cost. STL at 69 points with 8 expiring deals and only $9.84M profit are not desperate but are not in the race. At $600K, STL might accept a conditional late pick or a depth player. He's expiring, so this is a playoff rental with development upside if he re-signs.

**Savard** (ATL, C, 27, FACE 89, 48 points in 43 games, $1.00M expiring) is the better faceoff number than Reid but at a center position, which pairs with Sundin for playoff matchups. ATL at 72 points with 11 expiring are prioritizing Kovalchuk and Heatley. Savard is a secondary piece in their fire-sale. He folds into an ATL conversation at low marginal cost if one opens.

**Cammalleri** (LA, LW, 22, POTE 98, 1.17 ppg, $1.10M expiring) and **Frolov** (LA, LW, 22, POTE 96, 1.18 ppg, $1.10M expiring) carry the highest ceiling on this board. LA at 67 points with 15 expiring contracts are the deepest sellers in the league. But we have one 4th-rounder and every package is player-funded. A Belfour-plus-4th offer to LA for one of them is possible, but LA taking a 39-year-old at $6.50M on a non-contender is unlikely without a sweetener. Keep this alive but it's the lowest-probability deal on the list.

**Komisarek** (MTL, D, 23, 77 base, 83 TOUG, POTE 90, $1.10M expiring) is the blue-line development piece from the league's second-worst club. MTL at 55 points with 15 expiring deals are in full teardown. At $1.10M and POTE 90, if we re-sign him he fills the 24-29 bracket we currently have only twelve players in. But he's expiring, so it's a rental unless the GM re-signs him in July. Package: Svehla plus a 4th? No — Svehla should fetch a pick directly via the over-80 mechanic. Komisarek costs a depth player.

**Svehla** (36, 92 CHKG, $3.60M, 1 year expiring) is the other pick-recovery asset. Per the Feb 19 GM standing order, send him to a non-playoff team. Any of CGY, MTL, SJ, MIN, CHI would take a 92 CHKG blueliner for playoff insurance. Return: a 4th or 5th. This is the cleanest draft-capital recovery available and should happen regardless of whether other deals land.

## Trade construction

The question this phase answers: what do we hand over before March 19, and why does the other GM say yes? Two assets expire in July (Belfour at $6.50M, Svehla at $3.60M) and the 4th-rounder is our only pick. Every package must be player-funded and must send expiring value to teams who won't hurt us in April.

**Belfour to Colorado for Morris.** The GM already tested Colorado and they offered Hejduk. The March 5 note flags Morris as the better return: 26 years old, 85 base, 57 points in 65 games, $1.70M. Colorado lose both Morris and Skoula in July (from q112, both 1-year contracts), and they have a playoff hole in net. Belfour at 2.27 GAA and .916 in 21 games is the playoff insurance a 91-point team needs tonight. The payroll swap works: Colorado shed $1.70M and add $6.50M for the rest of this season, trivial against a contender's revenue. We remove $6.50M and add $1.70M, netting $4.80M of space for the Tier 1 renewals. Morris is re-signable at $2-2.5M in July. If Colorado refuse to move Morris specifically, Hejduk at 89 base and 31 is the fallback but fails the "locked for two years" test (1 year left, $5.10M). Test Morris first.

**Tucker plus the 4th to Ottawa for Havlat.** From q113, Ottawa at 65 points hold Alfredsson (92, $4.70M, expiring), Bonk (86, $3.40M, expiring), Smolinski (84, $2.40M, expiring), and Havlat (87, $900K, expiring). They cannot keep four top-nine forwards. Havlat is the cheapest and the most replaceable. Tucker at 92 CHKG and 88 TOUG gives them the physical wing they lack (their best checking forward is Fisher at 85, and the rest are 50-73). Tucker is 29 with two years left, so Ottawa get a roster piece, not a rental. We get a 23-year-old at 87 base who just scored 80 points in 63 games for $900K. If he re-signs in July at $3-4M, we've bought a second-line winger for a pick we can't otherwise spend. If he walks, the cost is Tucker (not lined all season, 1 point in 3 games) and a 4th.

**Svehla to a non-playoff team for a late pick.** From q114, Atlanta at 72 points have ten defensemen and zero at 80+ CHKG. They are the worst defensive depth in the league among teams with a full blueline. Per the March 4 GM correction, a non-contender is the right destination to avoid strengthening a rival. The over-80 expiring mechanic should extract a 4th or 5th from them. Svehla's $3.60M salary is the obstacle; ATL have room only if they've already shed salary. If ATL decline, try PHX at 74 (9 defensemen, 2 at 80+) or NYR at 76 (9 defensemen, 3 at 80+). Any non-playoff club satisfies the "not a rival" test.

**What to do if none land.** Dress Tucker every night as the Jackman-load fix (the role coverage confirms his 92 CHKG is free currency). Accept the single-faceoff-winner gap through April and target Savard (89 FACE, ATL, expiring) in July free agency. Belfour either stays as backup on a reduced offer or walks to retirement; the GM takes that risk knowingly. Svehla walks in July and the pick capital is lost. The season's trade deadline then ends with zero movement, which is survivable at 114 points but leaves the faceoff gap unsolved.

## Owed

**Monitoring Luongo availability and DiPietro ice time/development for goalie trade window** — this is the item the GM asked for on Jan 19 with a Feb 20 deadline. It is 22 days past that deadline and the job is now closeable.

**DiPietro** has transformed since my February reading. In mid-February he had 21 GP, 3.64 GAA, 84.9% SV. Now at 52 GP he carries 2.82 GAA and 87.1% SV with a 26-23 record. That's a full season's workload at a quality number, and NYI at 70 points in 69 games are a confirmed non-contender. The problem is the standing order from Jan 15: "a really good high-90s goalie." DiPietro's base overall is 79 and his displayed overall is 83. He does not meet that bar. He is a solid number-two or a trade piece for someone rebuilding, not a franchise starter by the test the GM set.

**Luongo** is already on the roster at 93 overall, 25 years old, $1.60M, 2 years left, 42 GP. The Jan 15 order closed this: "Luongo is arrived. Goalies are solved. Done." No availability question remains.

**What changed:** DiPietro's case went from "bad numbers, small sample" to "good numbers, full sample but still grade-deficient." The conclusion is unchanged but now rests on 52 games instead of 21. Theodore (MTL, 91 base, $5.50M expiring) remains the only player who satisfies the high-90s-from-a-non-contender test, and MTL at 55 points in 71 games is that non-contender. This monitoring task is complete: DiPietro is eliminated on grade, Theodore is the live target already flagged on March 5.

title: Coach's report — run 1, in-game 2005-03-14

# Coach's report — run 1, in-game 2005-03-14

Next game at VAN on Tuesday 15 March 2005.

## Development opportunity

With 11 games left and the club at 50-12-5-4 for 114 points, the question is whether the young players who haven't got their chances are still waiting, and whether we owe it to them to finish the season differently from how we started it.

**Spezza** is the loudest case. POTE 99, 37 games in 71, 7.5 MPG even when he dressed. I raised this five times through January and February. He's now been scratched for 34 consecutive games. Eleven games remain and he's 21. Even if the minutes target for the season is gone, he should not finish a year at 37 games with the highest scouting number on the roster.

**Stahle** is the same problem in smaller form. POTE 96, 20 years old, 4 games in 71. When he did play he got 17.8 MPG, so the coaching staff trusts him. He just isn't getting dressed. Four games all year is not a development plan; it's an accident.

**Colaiacovo** has the same POTE 99 and got 31 games at 17.9 MPG, so when he plays he's top-four minutes. 0.39 pts/g is respectable for a 22-year-old in his first full stretch. Thirty-one games is thin. He should be getting 45-plus by season's end.

**Chlup** at 60 GP, 16.5 MPG, 49 points and 0.82 pts/g is earning every shift he gets. **Nash** at 58 GP, 12.7 MPG, 35 points on the third line is doing the same. **Gaborik** at 71 GP, 20.2 MPG, 85 points needs nothing from me. No change for these three.

**Upshall** at 57 GP and 8.8 MPG on the fourth line with POTE 99 is getting games but not meaningful ones. Fixing that means bumping him above someone performing, and Nash (0.60 pts/g) and Chistov (0.33 pts/g but 13.2 MPG on third-pair D minutes) are both earning their spots. I'll leave it.

**Klesla** at 71 GP, 14.9 MPG, 0.37 pts/g is getting every game and not producing. That's a spot Colaiacovo could fill. But tonight is at Vancouver, a 35-21 club, and the standing order says maximize quality against opponents like this. Tonight holds. The swap is a conversation for the remaining stretch.

**Koltsov** at 23 is a trading chip, not a development case. His value is already falling (0.28 pts/g on the season). Nothing to add.

**Spacek** at 19, 48 GP, 0.33 pts/g, 7.9 MPG: his year is what it is. The target is dead, I've said so. He's a depth center getting depth minutes. No change tonight.

## Development trends

The question: who is getting better and who is getting worse between December 1st and now, and does that change any roster plans? The answer reshapes the defensive sell list and re-opens McCabe after I pulled him off it on March 4th.

**McCabe** I need to correct myself. The March 4 note said he recovered to 0.83 pts/g over 66 games and came off the sell list. The current reading shows him at 0.49 pts/g over 71 games. That means roughly zero points in the 47 games since December 1st. He is the weakest producing defenceman on the roster at 29 years old, on four years and $3M a year. He goes back on the sell list at the top. I was wrong on March 4th.

**Chlup** is the best story. 0.62 pts/g in 13 games at the first window, 0.87 over 60 games now, which means he is well above 0.87 in the recent games alone since that early rate drags the average down. He is on 18.0 MPG and 19 years old. He is a first-line centre by production.

**Kaberle** is the only defenceman whose rate went up: 0.54 to 0.64 pts/g, minutes from 19.4 to 21.8. At 27 he is entering his prime and pulling the top-pair job away from everyone else on the blue line. The GM's instinct to protect him is confirmed by the trend.

**Chistov** is moving in the right direction. 0.29 to 0.35 pts/g, minutes from 9.5 to 14.5. Slow, steady, 21 years old. He is earning a top-nine spot by the end of the year.

**Stahle** played 4 games at 17.8 MPG after not dressing once through January. That is the first sign since I raised this that someone noticed POTE 96 sitting on the bench. He needs another 20 games next season or this was a one-off.

**Nash** is the worry among the young forwards. 0.83 pts/g in 24 games, 0.44 over 58. The minutes barely moved at 12.6 MPG, so the production collapsed on ice he is still getting. At 20, the expected direction is up, and it is sharply down.

**Spezza** has 37 games played all season at 5.3 MPG, and the total minutes barely changed since December, meaning he played almost no meaningful shifts in the recent stretch. POTE 99 at 21 and the development year is over. I have raised this six times now.

**Jackman** confirms the March 5 finding: 0.65 to 0.39 pts/g on a flat 30 MPG. At 24, with that load, the production should be climbing. It is not. The system fit is wrong or the endurance is gone.

**Klesla** at 0.30 pts/g over 71 games at age 22. A second declining season. Minutes stayed at 15 MPG, so the lack of output is not a usage problem.

**Koltsov** at 0.28 pts/g over 35 games. The trading chip is evaporating. Every club sees the rate, not the October start.

The veterans all read as expected: Sundin from 1.46 to 0.94 at 34, Mogilny from 1.62 to 0.81 at 36, Roberts from 1.29 to 0.83 at 38. Still contributing, all three declining, and next season's top six cannot be built around them as-is.

## Morale watch

The room is healthy. Average morale sits at 92 with the entire core jumping +5 together, which tells me the wins are doing the lifting. Nobody is in the zone where I'd shuffle minutes to protect a man's headspace.

**Spezza** is the only name below 89 at 86, up 1 from the last save. He's been scratched for months and carries 7.5 MPG across 37 games with 15 points. The +1 means he's not sinking, but he's been pinned in the low 80s all season. At 21 he needs a real role somewhere; the good news is that's a roster-construction question for you, not something I can fix by nudging a line before Vancouver.

**Jackman** at 30.4 MPG is the heaviest load on the club. His morale is 99 and climbing, so no immediate concern, but at 24 with production trending down (0.38 recent from my notes), if that number ever starts sliding it'll be the minutes talking. Not a today problem.

Everyone else sits at 89 or above. The +5 spike across Sundin, Mogilny, Richards, Chlup, Afinogenov and the entire blue line confirms the winning streak is the driver. I would not touch anyone's role before Tuesday.

## Role composition

**The question:** are our units built from the right players for their jobs, and do we have enough of each role to staff them? The answer is mostly yes, with one known structural hole.

**L1 (Sundin, Roberts, Gaborik, Jackman, Fischer)** is textbook top-line construction. Sundin centers (90 faceoffs, 92 scoring), Gaborik provides the finish (98 scoring, 99 speed), Roberts and Fischer give checking support (both 83 checking), and Jackman (89 checking, 76 toughness) anchors the shutdown D pair behind them. Mean checking 81 is high for a first line. No change.

**L2 (Chlup, Mogilny, Afinogenov, McCabe, Kaberle)** is an offensive line with Chlup (79 faceoffs) developing at center. The 69 checking mean is low, but this unit's job is to score off Kaberle and McCabe's transition, and Mogilny (92 scoring) and Afinogenov (90 scoring, 91 playmaking) do that. Pairing McCabe (83 checking) with Kaberle satisfies the guide's "one offensive + one defensive D" rule for this pair. No change.

**L3 (Richards, Nash, Chistov, Eminger, Klesla)** — Richards centers at 74 faceoffs and 96 clutch, giving our third-best draw man to the bottom six. Chistov at 97 speed stretches the ice. Eminger and Klesla are developing D getting minutes on the third pair. Sound construction. No change.

**L4 (Spacek, Abid, Upshall)** — faceoff mean 51, best 52. This is the known structural void. No one on this line or available from the bench fixes it. It remains a roster problem, not an arrangement problem, and is already on record from March 7.

**K1 (Sundin, Roberts, Kaberle, Fischer)** carries the question mark. Kaberle is our pure offensive D; his inclusion on the penalty kill alongside his P1 role means he's carrying both special teams plus even strength. His 85 stamina is the second-highest on the roster, so he can absorb the load grade-wise, but the swap candidate would be Eminger or Klesla, neither of whom brings checking above 83 or zone-exit speed. Kaberle's puck-handling at least helps him clear the zone. Keep him.

**K2 (Chlup, McCabe, Jackman, Abid)** is our hardest unit: 83 checking mean, 90 best. Jackman (89), McCabe (83), Abid (71 toughness) — this line can forecheck and kill. Well built. No change.

**Roster gaps:** toughness tops out at Jackman 76. We have no true enforcer grade. Against physical teams this shows up as an inability to deter forechecks through contact. We have four players at 83+ checking, so the role of "fourth forward who kills and checks" is covered; the role of "fifth forward who changes the emotional temperature through hits" does not exist on this roster. I have not raised this because our checking depth is adequate and no cheap upgrade fixes the toughness ceiling — it is a draft-and-develop problem.

## Opponent matchup

**Bertuzzi is the whole team.** At 93 OVR with 99 deking and 97 puck control, he and Naslund (89 OVR) are Vancouver's first line, and their first line is the difference between a good team and a dangerous one. Their second line centres Morrison (82), then drops to 73 and 72. Everything dangerous runs through Bertuzzi and Naslund.

**The current matchup is already right.** Fischer/Jackman sit on D1, which auto-pairs with our L1 (Sundin/Gaborik/Roberts). When the GM puts L1 on ice, Fischer and Jackman are behind them — both at 90 checking, which is the pair that can handle Bertuzzi. No swap needed. The GM should just make sure L1 is the line out when Bertuzzi's unit is on the ice.

**Kaberle/McCabe on D2 against Morrison's line is clean.** Morrison at 82 is a playmaker (88 passing), not a power forward. Kaberle (69 checking) is the weaker defender, but McCabe (85 checking) covers, and Morrison's wingers are 73 and 71. No change.

**Eminger/Klesla on D3 against the Sedins is fine.** The Sedins at 72 and 73 are not going to beat Eminger (79 checking) or Klesla (77 checking). Their third line has no one above 74.

**Vancouver's power play is 31 for 210 (14.8%).** Worst unit on the sheet. Our PK with Roberts, Fischer, Sundin and Chlup on the first kill will eat it. No PK adjustment.

**Belfour** at 92 OVR is the right start, but per the standing order the GM needs to check the fatigue icon on screen before confirming. No fatigue flag appears in the brief, so he is likely fine, but the check is non-negotiable.

**No lineup changes.** The defensive pair slots already track Vancouver's line strength correctly. The game is won by keeping Bertuzzi and Naslund off the scoresheet, and Fischer/Jackman do that from D1 without any rearrangement.

**D evaluation (standing task #1):** Eminger at 75 OVR is still the weakest blue-liner by 7 points and stays at the top of the sell list. Klesla at 82 looks fine on the sheet but his season rate (0.38 pts/g at 22, flat minutes) says sell order two. McCabe at 82 is playing well — off the list, holds. Without per-game production data in this brief I cannot refresh the exact recent rates; the March 4 findings stand unless next week's numbers shift them.

## Owed

The standing job: how our defencemen have played and who should go at season's end. This is the 11th delivery since the GM set it on January 15.

**What's changed since March 11:** Jackman's collapse is no longer a recent window — it is his season. McCabe continues to prove he belongs on a long-term contract. Sell order is unchanged but Salo is now off the roster so it tightens to three names.

**Jackman** at 69 games, 33 points = 0.48 pts/g on 30.4 MPG. His March 5 recent window (0.38) has dragged the season from 0.65 down to 0.48, and that trend hasn't stopped. He's 24 and carrying the heaviest load on the team. Either the system is eating him alive or he's burned out from 30 minutes a night. This is now a genuine concern, not a watch-list item. If he holds 0.48 through the final 11 games, his role next season needs to change (fewer minutes, different partner) or he needs to be moved while he still has trade value at 24 and 84 OVR.

**McCabe** at 71 games, 57 points = 0.80 pts/g. Rock solid. The March 4 call (off sell list) is confirmed across the full body of work. Four years at $3.00M is steep for a 29-year-old, but he's producing at a first-pair rate and there's no argument to make.

**Fischer** at 66 games, 33 points = 0.50 pts/g, 0 PIM, $3.70M x 4. Keeper per GM standing order. No issue.

**Kaberle** at 63 games, 38 points = 0.60 pts/g, $1.90M x 1. Keeper per GM standing order. Needs a renewal conversation before the offseason, but that's the GM's assistant's problem.

**Eminger** at 53 games, 21 points = 0.40 pts/g, $1.20M x 1 (expiring). Still below the 0.45 threshold. My February 26 call stands: sell him before he walks for nothing. The recovery in February didn't hold and there's been no second one.

**Klesla** at 71 games, 26 points = 0.37 pts/g, $0.90M x 2. Essentially unchanged from February. At 22 with minutes flat at 14.9 and a declining trend across two seasons, he's the second name on the sell list. The money is cheap so the return will be modest, but two years at $0.90M for a bottom-pair player who won't improve is a waste of a roster spot.

**Colaiacovo** at 31 games, 12 points = 0.39 pts/g, $1.10M x 1. Not dressed. Development rotation per the GM's standing order. No sell recommendation — he's getting the minutes the GM is deliberately withholding from others.

**Sell order, updated:** Eminger (expiring, no recovery), Klesla (declining at 22, two years of cheap filler), then Colaiacovo only if the GM decides development rotation hasn't worked after next season.

**New concern:** Jackman. Not a sell candidate yet — 84 OVR and 30 MPG make him too valuable to dump — but the role needs adjustment or he's a sell next summer at a worse price than today.
